title: Ramadan: planning
hook: a plan for reading, prayer, charity and rest

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rajab and Sha'ban: a sacred month, then the month he fasted most outside Ramadan, a warmup before the door. Your line: getting ready. Did the habit you picked get its first minute? Today, the door opens. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-eight.

A sheet of paper taped to a fridge door, a few days before the new moon. Four words written across the top: reading, prayer, charity, rest. Under each one, a line or two. A portion of the Qur'an a day. Which nights at the mosque. Who gets the zakat, and when. What time the alarm goes off for the meal before dawn, and what time the phone goes off at night. It doesn't look holy. It looks like a schedule. But some families sit down and do exactly this before Ramadan, because a month can slip past on good intentions alone. Today: planning the month.
screen: `A SHEET OF PAPER, FOUR WORDS.` → `IT LOOKS LIKE A SCHEDULE.` → `A MONTH CAN SLIP PAST.`

segments.voice: Begin with reading, because the Qur'an itself ties the month to the book. Surah al-Baqarah, in Pickthall's words: "The month of Ramadan in which was revealed the Qur'an, a guidance for mankind, and clear proofs of the guidance, and the Criterion." Ibn 'Abbas reports in al-Bukhari that Jibril would meet the Prophet, peace be upon him, every night of Ramadan and go over the Qur'an with him. So a reading plan isn't an extra. It follows the habit Ibn 'Abbas describes. Second, charity, which the same report ties to the reading. Ibn 'Abbas says the Prophet was the most generous of people, and most generous of all in Ramadan when Jibril met him, more generous, he says, than a wind sent out. A plan for giving belongs on the sheet next to the plan for reading. Then prayer, and the nights: in another hadith in al-Bukhari, whoever stands in prayer through Ramadan out of faith and hoping for reward is forgiven past sins. Third, rest, the column people forget. The same verse in al-Baqarah says: "Allah desireth for you ease; He desireth not hardship for you." The month is meant to be hard enough to change you, not so hard it breaks you. In al-Bukhari, the Prophet tells people to eat the meal before dawn, because there's blessing in it. Sleep, food and water are part of the plan, not a failure of it. Fourth, look back at this week. The life cycle closed. Then the year opened: the sacred months, Muharram, Ashura, Rabi' al-Awwal, Rajab and Sha'ban. All of it walking toward this one month. A plan is how you arrive on purpose.
screen: `READING: THE MONTH OF THE BOOK.` · `GIVING, LIKE A WIND SENT OUT.` · `REST: ALLAH DESIRETH FOR YOU EASE.` · `A WEEK WALKING TOWARD ONE MONTH.`

segments.voice: The practice: write your Ramadan plan, starting in your head. Settle, and breathe. Picture the sheet of paper and the four words. Reading: one small, realistic amount a day. Prayer: one time of day you'll protect. Charity: one person or cause, and when. Rest: one thing you'll keep, sleep, water, a quiet hour. Keep each line short enough to actually do. If you won't fast, the same four words still work for any month you want to keep well. If you pray, you can ask for help with the plan. The bell holds the time.
Ramadan. The month of fasting, the month al-Baqarah says the Qur'an was revealed in, with room for reading, prayer, charity and rest. Today's word.
Your line: plan the month. Today, put the four lines on real paper or in your phone, and put it where you'll see it. Tomorrow, Ramadan: the family. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Muslims fast from dawn to sunset in Ramadan, and some make a plan beforehand for reading the Qur'an, night prayer, charity and zakat, and enough sleep and food at the pre-dawn meal, drawing on Qur'an 2:185 and hadiths in al-Bukhari.

trapdoor: what you thought: Ramadan is a month of not eating.
what it means: a month built around the Qur'an, with prayer, giving and rest planned in alongside the fast.
what a scholar hears: 2:185 tying the month to revelation and to ease, and Ibn 'Abbas's report in al-Bukhari of Jibril's nightly review and the Prophet's generosity.
